title: New theory of black holes solves problem of dark matter
subtitle: The evaporation of three cosmic mysteries
author: Phillip B. Levin
introduction: The last century of cosmological discovery has revolutionised our understanding of the universe, but as with many things in science, our proposed solutions to problems often soon turn into problems in their own right. Take the physical impossibility of spacetime singularities, the bizarre behaviour of black holes, and the invisible “dark matter” needed to explain the cosmos; as examples of such modern cosmological problems. Phillip B. Levin though, here argues, that all three of these problems can be neatly solved if we consider a new model of black holes – a model where black holes have no singularity.
body:
Over the last century, three questions have confounded the field of theoretical physics. What is the nature of the black hole singularity? What happens at the end of the evaporation process of a black hole? And what is dark matter?

There is remaining mystery in each question today. However, it turns out that all three questions can be connected by a surprisingly simple hypothesis: dark matter consists of the remnants of a very special kind of black hole – a black hole without a singularity – which formed in the very early universe. These nonsingular black holes evaporate like Stephen Hawking thought but then do something surprising: they stop heating up, instead cooling off to form remnants. Due to their special properties, these old and cold remnants may constitute all of the dark matter in the observable universe today, as explained in a new paper on the subject.

The first mystery concerns the nature of the singularity of a black hole. In 1915, Karl Schwarzschild discovered a solution to the Einstein Field Equations of General Relativity, describing a spacetime which contained two fascinating and unusual regions: the event horizon and the singularity. The event horizon marks a point of no return; any matter, as well as light, which crosses the horizon is forever trapped behind it, struggling with finite speed to escape the effect of infinite gravitation. The singularity, meanwhile, is the very region of infinite density and infinite gravity. An observer outside of the event horizon cannot see what lies on the other side and an observer who travels past the event horizon cannot return to tell the story of the singularity. It is no wonder that such a befitting name as “black hole” would occur to John Wheeler to describe Schwarzschild’s strange spacetime.

Albert Einstein argued that the presence of a singularity is deeply pathological for a physical theory, saying, “A singularity brings so much arbitrariness into a theory that it actually nullifies its laws.”

Indeed, the mystery of the black hole, especially the region of the singularity, has held a powerful allure, attracting many to wonder what happens at this special region of spacetime, where gravity becomes infinite. Theoretical physicists have accepted by consensus for some time now that the singularity indicates the breakdown of the classical description of the black hole, and to truly understand what’s going on we require a quantum theory of gravitation.

Despite the fact that a singularity explicitly lurks in Schwarzschild’s solution, the idea that spacetime might possess an edge or boundary at which the curvature becomes infinite was long supposed to be a pathology of general relativity. Writing in 1935 about the presence of infinities in physical theories, Albert Einstein argued that the presence of a singularity is deeply pathological for a physical theory, saying, “A singularity brings so much arbitrariness into a theory that it actually nullifies its laws.” Einstein, of course, did not believe that black holes existed, so one may be tempted to ignore his line of thinking when it comes to the singularity of a black hole. But one should be cautious to throw out his underlying philosophy of physics. While Einstein would later reject the existence of black holes, perhaps he is right that complete physical theories should not contain singularities. If he’s right, then the black hole singularity is a mirage; it doesn’t exist at all.

From the observation by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2022 of Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole at the centre of our Milky Way Galaxy, we know something that Einstein did not: black holes do exist. But perhaps Einstein knew something that has since been neglected in theoretical physics: the singularity, which is represented by infinity, is non-physical because it cannot be observed. The unobservability of the singularity is true in two senses. The first sense is that the singularity lies on the other side of the event horizon, and thus an observer from outside the black hole cannot observe it, and meanwhile an observer who travels to the singularity to make sure of its existence cannot observe it and then return to tell the world about it. For this reason, even the observations of Sagittarius A* by the Event Horizon Telescope do not provide a measurement of the singularity itself. The second sense in which the singularity is unobservable is even more profound: it is not possible to measure infinity, and thus the infinite gravitation associated with the region of the black hole singularity cannot be measured or observed. It is because of this second reason that one should be inclined to believe that the singularity is unphysical and that Einstein’s thought about singularities was wise.

Applying Einstein’s criteria for a complete physical theory suggests that real black holes do not have a singularity. It turns out that one can construct theoretical descriptions of black holes that do not have a singularity. In 1968, James Bardeen, a student of Richard Feynman, discovered the first nonsingular black hole solution. A general property of these black holes is that they avoid the singularity theorems of Stephen Hawking and Roger Penrose, proved in late 1960 and early 1970, which show how gravitational collapse leads to the formation of spacetime singularities. In 2018, Damien Easson of Arizona State University showed how the formation of the singularity can be avoided by limiting the curvature of spacetime, leading to a nonsingular Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole. An observer outside of the event horizon of such a black hole sees what appears as a Schwarzschild black hole in an expanding universe. Meanwhile, an observer who enters the black hole finds on the other side of the event horizon a baby universe which is also expanding. This black hole interior has finite gravitation and no singularity.

SUGGESTED VIEWING Cosmology needs philosophy With Bjørn Ekeberg

The second mystery concerns the end-state of black hole evaporation. In 1974, Stephen Hawking found something remarkable: black holes are not perfectly black after all. Hawking showed using quantum field theory that a black hole evaporates, producing radiation with a temperature inversely proportional to the mass of the black hole. That is, Hawking showed that black holes are not stable. Any black hole, Hawking showed, has a finite lifetime, radiating until it evaporates completely. The complete evaporation of black holes leads to a number of puzzles, including the infamous black hole information paradox, but perhaps as important (though this fact has not been discussed as much in the popular media) is another singularity problem: because the temperature of a black hole depends inversely on its mass, an evaporating black hole near zero-mass radiates an infinite temperature. We know from our previous discussion of singularities in physical theories that this is problematic, suggesting perhaps that towards the end of Hawking evaporation, something special must happen to the thermodynamics of a black hole to avoid such a black hole explosion on the order of infinity. If infinite temperatures are to be avoided, it seems that the evaporation process must conclude in the formation of a remnant with finite or zero temperature.

A natural candidate is the nonsingular Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole, otherwise known as a dilation gravity black hole or DGBH, which arises out of string theoretic quantum gravity. This black hole’s thermodynamic behaviour, as shown by the orange curve in the figure, is similar to that of a Schwarzschild black hole, its temperature increasing as the mass decreases, until a minimum mass is reached, at which point the nonsingular black hole reaches its maximum temperature, and then as it decreases in mass cools off until it reaches either a finite or zero temperature. The temperature and mass relationship described is a general property of a class of nonsingular back holes, making these nonsingular black holes excellent candidates for the evaporation process of a black hole whose end-state is a cooling remnant.

A class of nonsingular black holes have different evaporation profiles compared to the Schwarzschild black hole.

The third mystery is the identity of dark matter. In 1933, Fritz Zwicky postulated the existence of dunkle Materie, German for dark matter, to explain why the observed matter of the Coma cluster of galaxies was insufficient to account for its gravitation. The reality of dark matter was further supported in Vera Rubin’s observation in the ‘70s that the rotational speeds of outer galaxies are too high for the amount of observed visible matter. For nearly a hundred years, the evidence for dark matter has continued to accumulate, coming from studies of gravitational lensing, galaxy rotation curves, the cosmic microwave background, and the formation of cosmic structures. According to general relativity, dark, non-baryonic matter is estimated to comprise 25% of the total matter of the observable universe. However, despite decades of expensive observational and experimental searches of dark matter candidates, such as WIMPS and axions, there is no conclusive evidence for the identity of the elusive dark matter.

In recent years, there has been a renewed interest in the possibility of primordial black holes as a dark matter candidate. These black holes may have formed early in the universe, playing the role of dark matter. Many studies have shown that primordial black holes are an excellent model for dark matter. The mass range of primordial black hole dark matter has been constrained by studies of evaporation, microlensing, gravitational waves, dynamics, and accretion. The bottom-end of this mass range is set by evaporation constraints.

Observational constraints of primordial black holes as dark matter. Colored regions are excluded as viable. The x-axis is the mass of primordial black holes (measured in grams on the top and measured in solar masses on the bottom). The y-axis is the fraction of primordial black holes that are dark matter. For example, when the fraction is 1 (100), this means that all the dark matter is made up of primordial black holes.

It is here that we see how all three mysteries may be related: this range can be naturally extended by the hypothesis that primordial black hole dark matter should include nonsingular black holes specifically. If the Hawking evaporation process continues until a black hole disappears, then any primordial black holes of mass less than 10 15 grams would have already evaporated entirely. However, if the evaporation process of a real astrophysical black hole is like that of a nonsingular black hole, then primordial black holes with masses much less than 1015 g can continue to exist today. This is because nonsingular black holes evaporate more slowly, cooling off at the end of their lives, forming a kind of remnant, which observational searches of dark matter, thus far, have not known to look for.

In particular, the nonsingular Schwarzschild-de Sitter black hole is an ideal candidate for primordial black hole dark matter because at the end of its lifetime, it forms a remnant whose mass depends on the fundamental length scale. It is thought that fundamental scale should be the Planck length, thus this nonsingular black hole evaporates until it reaches the Planck mass, which is 10-5 g. Thus nonsingular black holes extend the viable mass range of primordial black holes by twenty orders of magnitude below the previously-thought minimum mass based on complete evaporation of a black hole.

We know that the fraction of primordial black holes that make up dark matter is inversely proportional to the square root of the lightest black hole that might still exist today. Assuming the traditional argument from the Hawking evaporation calculation, primordial black holes must have masses greater than 1015 g. As a consequence of this larger value of mass, the usual primordial black holes are thought unlikely to constitute all of the dark matter in the observable universe but rather just a fraction of it. This is not true of nonsingular black holes, however. Nonsingular black hole remnants on the order of the Planck mass can comprise all of the dark matter because their masses are many orders of magnitude smaller.

Remarkably, these three mysteries are intertwined in the hypothesis that dark matter consists of nonsingular black holes which are the end-state of black hole evaporation. These nonsingular black holes could have formed primordially, shortly after the end of inflation. Nonsingular black holes are ideal candidates for primordial dark matter because they have no spacetime or gravitation singularity nor do they emit infinite temperatures as they evaporate, thus resolving the first two mysteries. Rather, the theoretical description of their spacetime geometry is well defined at all points and the end-state of their evaporation process is a cold remnant. These nonsingular black hole remnants interact only gravitationally with other matter, thus they resolve the third mystery, being a kind of dark matter. Due to the fact that they are small and weakly interacting, they could have survived until today, without accreting matter and growing as do other black holes, instead lingering as dark matter in the form of cold nonsingular black hole remnants. Because of their small masses, they can comprise potentially all of the dark matter required by observations.

A particularly compelling aspect of this new theory is in its explanation of why these searches may have failed: we have not known to look for such small and cold black holes.

Indeed, there is a trifecta resolution: curing the singularity of the black hole naturally tells us about the end state of black hole evaporation and solves the problem of dark matter.

Good science is an interplay between theory and observation. While this resolution is promising on theoretical grounds, the next step is that of finding good observational evidence for it. Due to being weakly interacting and cold, nonsingular black holes face observational challenges similar to other dark matter candidates. The unique thermodynamic behavior of nonsingular black holes will likely play an important role in searching for them, as this is one of their distinguishing features. Experimental and observational searches for dark matter, including primordial black hole dark matter, have been underway now for decades without success. The search for dark matter, like all observational searches, depends on theory. A particularly compelling aspect of this new theory is in its explanation of why these searches may have failed: we have not known to look for such small and cold black holes.

Perhaps the lack of success is because dark matter is not, after all, a type of subatomic particle, but a very different sort of entity with a very different signature.

While it’s possible that previous dark matter searches have missed nonsingular black hole remnants due to their unexpectedly small masses, there is also reason to be hopeful about future observational and experimental searches of dark matter discovering these black hole remnants.  A new and tantalizing approach from Carlo Rovelli, Marios Christodoulou, and Alejandro Perez, for example, gives some idea about the possibilities, inspiring hope for the search for nonsingular black hole remnants as dark matter. This year, these authors proposed a quantum gravity experiment which may be capable of directly detecting Planck-mass dark matter using quantum interference. Such an idea may be fruitful for the search for Planck-mass nonsingular black hole remnants as well.

Thus far physicists have mostly focused their search for dark matter candidates on novel fundamental particles, from photinos to axions. Perhaps the lack of success is because dark matter is not, after all, a type of subatomic particle, but a very different sort of entity with a very different signature. Primordial nonsingular black hole remnants, tiny but still massive, may be the dark matter we’ve been searching for. Now the challenge is to find them.
